pages.text: An anvil is the main tool of the smith: it shapes ingots and welds them. Anvils serve two jobs, $(l:metalworking/anvils#working)Working$(), which forms one piece of metal into another, and $(l:metalworking/anvils#welding)Welding$(), which fuses two pieces into one.
An anvil is crafted from $(thing)Double Ingots$() of its metal. For the first one, $(l:metalworking/anvils#welding)weld$() the double ingots on a $(l:getting_started/primitive_anvils)Stone Anvil$().

Every anvil has a $(thing)Tier$(), which says what it can work and weld. It works metals of its own tier and welds those one tier up.$(li)$(bold)VI$(): Blue and Red Steel$(li)$(bold)V$(): Black Steel$(li)$(bold)IV$(): Steel$(li)$(bold)III$(): Wrought Iron$(li)$(bold)II$(): Bronze, Black Bronze, Bismuth Bronze$(li)$(bold)I$(): Copper, also arsenical$(li)$(bold)0$(): Stone
To work an item, use the anvil to open its interface. The item goes in the right input slot. You also need a hammer, in the hammer slot or in your main hand; it wears as you work.
pages.title: Working

pages.text: Then choose a $(thing)Plan$(), which says what item you make. $(item)$(k:key.attack)$() the scroll button and pick the item. The interface returns with the scroll showing your plan, and the $(thing)Rules$() and $(thing)Target$() filled in.

The middle bar has two markers. The $(2)green$() one is your progress, the $(4)red$() one is the target. Bring progress onto the target with the green and red action buttons, each of which moves it by a set step.
pages.title: Targets

pages.text: $(2)Green$() actions always move the progress $(bold)right$() and $(4)red$() ones $(bold)left$(). If it leaves the bar, the item is overworked and lost. And at the end the $(thing)rules$() must hold as well.
Rules are the two or three symbols over the bar: actions that must fall at set moments. For example $(2)Bend Second Last$() means the second action from the end has to be a $(2)Bend$().
pages.title: Working Rules

pages.text: Your last three actions show under the rules, and a rule turns green when met. You succeed when all are met. Mind the $(l:core_mechanics/heating)temperature$() too: metal can be worked only while the tooltip says $(bold)Can Work$(). Take it out and reheat it as often as needed.
Working takes many steps, and efficiency is rewarded. Some items, such as tool heads, made in few steps carry a $(thing)Forging Bonus$() into the tool built from them.
pages.title: Forging bonuses

pages.text: Best first:$(li)perfectly forged$(li)expertly forged$(li)well forged$(li)poorly forged$(br2)A bonus makes a tool last longer, dig faster or hit harder, depending on the tool.
pages.title: Perfectly Forged

pages.text: $(thing)Cast Iron$() is brittle: it cannot be forged into rods or sheets nor welded, only cast.$(br2)Copper from tetrahedrite is $(thing)arsenical$(). It is forged and welded as copper, on a copper anvil made of its own double ingot, but what is made of it carries a mark, and melts back into arsenical copper, never into pure copper.
pages.title: What is not forged

pages.text: Welding fuses two items into a new one. It is the same on a stone anvil as on a metal one.$(br2)Put both items on the anvil, using them on it or by the interface, in the two left slots.
pages.title: Welding

pages.text: You also need at least one $(l:metalworking/flux)Flux$() on the anvil, plain or borax. Then, while both items are $(l:core_mechanics/heating)hot enough$() and the tooltip says $(bold)Can Weld$(), strike the anvil with any $(thing)Hammer$(). The items fuse. Take them out with an empty hand and $(item)$(k:key.use)$().
